subject: Engineering Mathematics
summary: limits, continuity, mean value theorems, maxima-minima, definite and improper integrals, multiple integrals
next_day: Theory of Machines, Dynamics of Linkages & Flywheels

questions.text: The value of lim<sub>x→0</sub> (e<sup>x</sup> − e<sup>−x</sup> − 2x) / (x − sin x) is
solution: Concept: For a 0/0 limit, expand numerator and denominator in Maclaurin series and compare the lowest powers.
ex − e−x = 2 sinh x = 2x + x3/3 + …, so the numerator = x3/3 + O(x5).
x − sin x = x3/6 + O(x5).
Exam tip: L'Hospital needs three rounds here; the series method settles it in two lines. Keep ex, sin x, cos x, ln(1+x) series to the x3 term at your fingertips.

questions.text: The value of lim<sub>x→∞</sub> (1 + 3/x)<sup>2x</sup> (round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: 1∞ form: lim fg = eL, where L = lim g·(f − 1).
Here f − 1 = 3/x and g = 2x, so L = lim 2x · (3/x) = 6.
Limit = e6 = 403.43
Exam tip: Remember lim (1 + a/x)bx = eab. Writing the answer as 1 (because 1 raised to anything is 1) is the classic trap.

questions.text: For f(x) = x|x|, which statement is correct at x = 0?
opts: f is continuous but not differentiable
solution: Concept: Test differentiability with the left and right difference quotients.
f(x) = x<sup>2</sup> for x ≥ 0 and −x<sup>2</sup> for x < 0, so f(0) = 0 and f is continuous.
Right derivative: lim<sub>h→0+</sub> h·h / h = 0. Left derivative: lim<sub>h→0−</sub> h(−h)/h = 0.
Both equal 0, so f is differentiable with f′(0) = 0. (In fact f′(x) = 2|x|, which is not differentiable at 0, so f″(0) does not exist.)
Exam tip: |x| has a corner at 0, but multiplying by x flattens it. Do not mark every function containing |x| as non-differentiable.

questions.text: The value of c given by Lagrange's mean value theorem for f(x) = √x on the interval [4, 9] is ______ (round off to two decimal places)
solution: Concept: Lagrange's MVT: f′(c) = [f(b) − f(a)] / (b − a) for some c in (a, b).
Exam tip: Always check that c lands inside the open interval; if it does not, re-check the algebra.

questions.text: For f(x) = sin x + cos x on [0, π/2], the value of c given by Rolle's theorem is
solution: Concept: Rolle's theorem: f continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b) and f(a) = f(b) ⇒ f′(c) = 0 for some c in (a, b).
f′(x) = cos x − sin x = 0 → tan c = 1 → c = π/4
Exam tip: Verify f(a) = f(b) first. π/3 and π/6 are tempting but give f′(c) ≠ 0.

questions.text: The absolute maximum value of f(x) = x<sup>3</sup> − 6x<sup>2</sup> + 9x + 15 on the closed interval [0, 5] is ______
solution: Concept: On a closed interval, the absolute maximum is the largest of f at the critical points and at the two end points.
Absolute maximum = 35, at the end point x = 5 (figure).
Exam tip: 19 is only the local maximum. A local maximum need not be the absolute maximum; always evaluate the end points.

questions.text: The minimum value of f(x, y) = x<sup>4</sup> + y<sup>4</sup> − 4xy is
solution: Concept: Stationary points from fx = fy = 0; classify with r = fxx, s = fxy, t = fyy: rt − s2 > 0 and r > 0 → minimum.
f<sub>x</sub> = 4x<sup>3</sup> − 4y = 0 → y = x<sup>3</sup>; f<sub>y</sub> = 4y<sup>3</sup> − 4x = 0 → x<sup>9</sup> = x → x = 0, ±1.
Stationary points: (0, 0), (1, 1), (−1, −1).
At (0, 0): r = t = 0, s = −4 → rt − s<sup>2</sup> = −16 < 0 → saddle point.
Exam tip: f(0, 0) = 0 is not the minimum: (0, 0) is a saddle. Always run the rt − s2 test.

questions.text: The minimum value of x<sup>2</sup> + y<sup>2</sup> subject to the constraint x + 2y = 10 is ______
solution: Concept: Lagrange multipliers: ∇f = λ∇g at the constrained optimum.
2x = λ and 2y = 2λ → y = 2x.
Substitute in x + 2y = 10: 5x = 10 → x = 2, y = 4.
Minimum = 22 + 42 = 20
Exam tip: Check geometrically: it is the square of the distance from the origin to the line, (10/√5)2 = 20.

questions.text: The value of ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>π/2</sup> √(sin x) / (√(sin x) + √(cos x)) dx is
solution: Concept: King's property: ∫0a f(x) dx = ∫0a f(a − x) dx.
Replacing x by π/2 − x swaps sin and cos: I = ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>π/2</sup> √(cos x) / (√(cos x) + √(sin x)) dx.
Adding the two forms: 2I = ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>π/2</sup> 1 dx = π/2.
Exam tip: Whenever sin and cos appear symmetrically over [0, π/2], the answer is half the interval length.

questions.text: The value of ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>π</sup> x sin<sup>2</sup>x dx is ______ (round off to two decimal places)
solution: Concept: ∫0a x f(x) dx = (a/2) ∫0a f(x) dx when f(a − x) = f(x).
sin<sup>2</sup>(π − x) = sin<sup>2</sup>x, so I = (π/2) ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>π</sup> sin<sup>2</sup>x dx.
∫<sub>0</sub><sup>π</sup> sin<sup>2</sup>x dx = π/2 (average value ½ over a full period).
Exam tip: This property removes the x factor without integration by parts.

questions.text: The value of the improper integral ∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>∞</sup> dx / (x<sup>2</sup> + 2x + 5) is
solution: Concept: Complete the square and use ∫ dx/(u2 + a2) = (1/a) tan−1(u/a).
x<sup>2</sup> + 2x + 5 = (x + 1)<sup>2</sup> + 2<sup>2</sup>.
The integrand behaves like 1/x<sup>2</sup> at both ends, so the integral converges.
Exam tip: Over (−∞, ∞) the shift x + 1 does not change the limits; only a (here 2) matters: answer = π/a.

questions.text: The value of ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>∞</sup> x<sup>4</sup> e<sup>−x<sup>2</sup></sup> dx is ______ (round off to three decimal places)
solution: Concept: Gamma function: Γ(n) = ∫0∞ tn−1 e−t dt, Γ(n + 1) = nΓ(n), Γ(½) = √π.
Put t = x<sup>2</sup>, x = t<sup>1/2</sup>, dx = dt / (2t<sup>1/2</sup>): I = ½ ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>∞</sup> t<sup>3/2</sup> e<sup>−t</sup> dt = ½ Γ(5/2).
Exam tip: General result: ∫0∞ xm e−x2 dx = ½ Γ((m + 1)/2).

questions.text: The region of integration of ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>4</sup> ∫<sub>y/2</sub><sup>√y</sup> f(x, y) dx dy is shown in the figure. On reversing the order of integration, the integral becomes
solution: Concept: Sketch the region from the given limits, then read the new limits from a strip drawn in the other direction.
Inner limits x = y/2 (the line y = 2x) and x = √y (the parabola y = x<sup>2</sup>); they meet at (0, 0) and (2, 4).
For a vertical strip at x (0 ≤ x ≤ 2): y runs from the parabola y = x<sup>2</sup> (lower) to the line y = 2x (upper).
New integral = ∫02 ∫x22x f dy dx. Check with f = 1: area = ∫02 (2x − x2) dx = 4/3 by both orders.
Exam tip: Option (A) swaps the curves (it gives −4/3 for f = 1). Test any reversal with f = 1: both orders must give the same positive area.

questions.text: The value of ∬<sub>R</sub> e<sup>−(x<sup>2</sup> + y<sup>2</sup>)</sup> dx dy, where R is the disc x<sup>2</sup> + y<sup>2</sup> ≤ 1, is ______ (round off to three decimal places)
solution: Concept: For circular regions, switch to polar coordinates: x2 + y2 = r2, dx dy = r dr dθ.
I = ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>2π</sup> ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>1</sup> e<sup>−r<sup>2</sup></sup> r dr dθ.
Inner: ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>1</sup> r e<sup>−r<sup>2</sup></sup> dr = ½(1 − e<sup>−1</sup>) = 0.3161.
Exam tip: The Jacobian r is what makes e−r2 integrable. Over the whole plane the same steps give π, the basis of ∫−∞∞ e−x2 dx = √π.

questions.text: The volume of the solid bounded by the paraboloid z = 4 − x<sup>2</sup> − y<sup>2</sup> and the plane z = 0 (shown) is ______ (round off to two decimal places)
solution: Concept: Volume = ∬ (height) dA over the base region; use polar coordinates for a circular base.
The paraboloid meets z = 0 on the circle x<sup>2</sup> + y<sup>2</sup> = 4, so the base is a disc of radius 2 and height = 4 − r<sup>2</sup>.
V = ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>2π</sup> ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> (4 − r<sup>2</sup>) r dr dθ = 2π [2r<sup>2</sup> − r<sup>4</sup>/4]<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> = 2π(8 − 4) = 8π
Exam tip: A paraboloid cap is exactly half of its circumscribing cylinder: ½ × π(2)2 × 4 = 8π. A quick check worth remembering.
